speaker: S1
text: Today: the Fourier transform. The core idea — any reasonable signal can be written as a sum of sinusoids, and the transform tells you how much of each frequency is present.

speaker: S1
text: Formally, F of omega equals the integral of f of t times e to the minus i omega t, dt, over all time. Think of it as correlating your signal against every possible frequency.

speaker: S1
text: Example one: a pure sine at five hertz. Its transform is two spikes, at plus and minus five hertz. Nothing else. That's the whole point — one frequency in, one pair of spikes out.

speaker: S1
text: Example two: a square wave. You get spikes at the fundamental and all odd harmonics, falling off as one over n. This is why square waves sound buzzy — they carry infinite harmonics.

speaker: S1
text: Key property for the exam: convolution in time is multiplication in frequency. Filtering is just multiplying the spectrum by a window. This will be on the midterm.

speaker: S1
text: The duality trips people up: a signal narrow in time is wide in frequency, and vice versa. A perfect impulse contains every frequency equally. Sit with that until it feels obvious.

speaker: S1
text: Next lecture we do the discrete version, the DFT, and why the FFT makes it fast enough to matter.
